text.t: ATP synthase is a machine of two rotary motors; this file is only the F1 head, the part that makes ATP.
The F0 motor that sits in the membrane is not in this file.
Chain B is one of the three beta subunits of the F1 head.
Here it holds ADP and a phosphate, the two pieces that get joined into ATP.
Chain A is an alpha subunit, and in this crystal it holds an ATP with a magnesium ion.
Chain G is the gamma subunit, the axle in the middle of the head.
As the axle turns, its odd shape forces the surrounding subunits through the steps of making ATP.
The full head has three alpha and three beta subunits around the axle, and in this structure all three beta subunits hold a nucleotide.

does.t: ATP synthase builds most of the ATP that powers your cells.
It uses a flow of hydrogen ions across a membrane to join ADP and phosphate into ATP.

shape.t: Hydrogen ions flowing through the F0 motor in the membrane spin a rotor, which turns the axle.
The turning axle forces the F1 head through three shapes: one binds ADP and phosphate, one forms the new bond, and one opens to release ATP.
Run backwards, the same F1 motor can break down ATP to spin the axle the other way.

text.t: ATP synthase sits in the inner membrane of mitochondria, where hydrogen ions flow back through it into the matrix.
This one comes from rat liver.

history.who: M.A. Bianchet, J. Hullihen, P.L. Pedersen and L.M. Amzel

text.t: This rat liver F1 structure was solved by X-ray crystallography at 2.8 angstroms, with nucleotide levels like those inside cells.
Big machines like ATP synthase are often solved in parts, and cryo-electron microscopy has since shown the whole machine.

compare.t: The part in this file, one alpha, one beta and the axle, measures about 13.6 nm from end to end.
The ATP it makes measures about 1.7 nm, so the machine is far bigger than its product.

text.t: ADP held by a beta subunit.
An ATP held by the alpha subunit.
